title: Diffusion Language Models as Open Quantum Systems
authors: Akinori Tanaka, Yukinao Akamatsu, Takuki Tomita, Yuji Hirono
abstract: Diffusion language models generate text by reversing a classical diffusion process over token sequences. We show that their continuous-time forward and reverse dynamics can be embedded in the framework of open quantum systems, which describes quantum systems interacting with their environment. This connection provides a basis for extending diffusion sampling to superpositions of sentence states and for modifying the underlying generation dynamics. We construct a $τ$-leaping unraveling scheme that simulates stochastic trajectories of these states while updating multiple token positions at each step. This enables generation conditioned on superposed prompts or thoughts, which we call Superposition of Prompts (SoP) and Superposition of Thoughts (SoT). The same formulation yields Quantum-Inspired Remasking (QIR): perturbing the masked-diffusion dynamics produces a confidence-based rule for revising previously generated tokens. Experiments with pretrained diffusion language models show that superposition-based generation can retain information from conditioning components not selected at the final measurement, while QIR improves LLM-assessed text quality when applied at an appropriate stage of generation.
summary: This paper maps the process of text generation via diffusion models onto the physics of open quantum systems described by the Lindblad equation. It introduces methods like Superposition of Prompts (SoP) and Quantum-Inspired Remasking (QIR) by leveraging this quantum formalism. The results show that this quantum perspective allows for richer, more controlled generation processes than standard diffusion models.
main_problem: The paper embeds the dynamics of diffusion language models into the framework of open quantum systems to extend generation capabilities.
main_result: Superposition-based generation (SoP/SoT) can retain information from unselected conditioning components, and Quantum-Inspired Remasking (QIR) improves text quality.
method: The authors use the Lindblad equation to model the open quantum system dynamics and construct a $\tau$-leaping unraveling scheme for stochastic simulation.
model_or_system: The system is a diffusion language model whose dynamics are mapped onto an open quantum system governed by the Lindblad equation. Superpositions of sentence states are treated as basis states in the Hilbert space.
key_observables: Generative perplexity (GenPPL), token-frequency entropy, CoLA acceptability score, and Qwen preference scores.
important_parameters: The remasking parameter $\gamma$ ($0 \le \gamma \le 1$) and the masking/update factor $\beta$ are key parameters analyzed.
main_assumptions: The stochastic unraveling requires a final projective measurement, and the authors do not claim a quantum speedup or provide a quantum circuit implementation.
figures_summary: Figure 6 shows text-quality metrics (GenPPL, Entropy, CoLA, Qwen preference) across different generation checkpoints, while Figure 7 quantifies excess long-token-sequence repetition.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the embedding of discrete diffusion models into the Lindblad framework, details the $\tau$-leaping unraveling for superpositions (SoP/SoT), and then empirically evaluates the resulting generation techniques, including QIR, using various text quality metrics.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, mathematically rigorous framework connecting modern generative AI (diffusion models) to the established formalism of open quantum systems, which is highly relevant for theoretical physicists studying non-unitary evolution.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: A superposition of sentence states viewed as an open quantum system interact- ing with its environment.

Figure 2: Sampling by stochastic unraveling followed by projective measurement. The ensemble of pure-state trajectories reproduces the corresponding density-operator dynamics, while the final measurement yields a discrete token sequence.

Figure 3: Cosine similarity of SEDD-small outputs to forest-only (horizontal) and snow-only (vertical) reference texts, computed using MiniLM embeddings. Green and blue show single-condition baselines; gray shows SoP outputs with forest (left) or snow (right) selected at final measurement. Superposition increases average similarity to the unselected condition.

Figure 4: Component weight p(i = 1) for masked and uniform SEDD at two coefficient- update exponents. Rows show forest/city(key__forest_city in Table 3) and past/fu- ture(package__past_future in Table 3); each panel contains 120 trajectories. Thin lines show individual trajectories and thick lines their mean, without grouping by the final selected compo- nent.

Figure 5: Mean trajectory-level Shannon entropy for the same SEDD experiments with forest/c- ity(key__forest_city in Table 3) and past/future(package__past_future in Table 3). Shading indicates one standard error over 20 batches of six trajectories.
